O imperativo afirmativo de tú e de usted: The affirmative imperative of tú and usted
PASSO 1: o imperativo serve para dar uma: STEP 1: the imperative is used to give an instruction, ask for something, invite, or give advice: «Mira», «Escucha», «Pasa». STEP 2: for «tú», the affirmative form is the same as the «él, ella» present-tense form. «Habla» (from hablar), «come» (from comer), «escribe» (from escribir). English's whole imperative, by contrast, is just the bare infinitive with no subject at all — "Look," "Listen," "Wait" — the same single form whether you're talking to one person, several people, a friend, or a stranger. Spanish's split between «tú» and «usted» forms, and the eight irregular «tú» forms coming up next, have no counterpart in English's one-size-fits-all imperative. STEP 3: verbs that change the stem vowel in the present do the same in the imperative: «cierra» (from cerrar), «vuelve» (from volver), «pide» (from pedir), «sigue» (from seguir). STEP 4: eight verbs have an irregular «tú» imperative, and you just have to memorize them: venir → «ven», decir → «di», hacer → «haz», ir → «ve», poner → «pon», salir → «sal», ser → «sé», tener → «ten». STEP 5: for «usted», you don't use the present-tense form; you use the present subjunctive. As a shortcut, just switch the ending's vowel. -ar verbs end in -e instead: «hable», «mire», «espere». -er and -ir verbs end in -a instead: «coma», «escriba», «abra». STEP 6: the «usted» irregulars follow the «yo» present: «venga», «diga», «haga», «vaya», «ponga», «salga», «sea», «tenga». STEP 7: for «ustedes» (more than one person), add «-n»: «hablen», «coman», «escriban». STEP 8: pronouns go after the verb and attach to it: «Escúchame», «Dime», «Siéntate». When you attach the pronoun, the written accent keeps the stress where it was: «escucha → escúchame», «cierra → ciérrala». STEP 9: the imperative only needs «por favor» to sound polite: «Pasa, por favor», «Espere un momento, por favor».
em português, o imperativo de «você» usa: Pronoun attachment is the other piece with no English parallel: English "listen to me" or "sit down" never attaches a pronoun onto the verb itself or shifts its stress — the pronoun is just a separate word that comes after, same as everywhere else in English. Spanish gluing «me» onto «escucha» to make «escúchame», with an added accent mark to keep the stress in place, is a mechanic you'll have to build from scratch.

PASSO 1: para negar uma ordem, a forma d: STEP 1: to negate a command, the «tú» form changes: you don't use the affirmative imperative. You write «no» + the present subjunctive form: «no hables», «no comas», «no escribas». STEP 2: how it's formed: -ar verbs swap «-as» for «-es», and -er and -ir verbs swap «-es» for «-as». Start from the «tú» present form: hablas → hables; comes → comas; escribes → escribas. This is new ground for an English speaker: English's negative imperative is just "don't" + the exact same bare infinitive you'd use affirmatively — "don't talk," "don't eat" — with no vowel swap and no subjunctive at all. STEP 3: with «usted» and «ustedes», the negative form is the same as the affirmative, with «no» in front: «no hable», «no coma», «no hablen». STEP 4: with «vosotros» (Spain), the affirmative is formed by swapping the infinitive's final «-r» for «-d»: «hablad», «comed», «escribid». The negative is «no» + subjunctive: «no habléis», «no comáis», «no escribáis». STEP 5: «ir» is the only exception to the «vosotros» affirmative: «id». STEP 6: in reflexive verbs, «vosotros» drops the «-d» before «-os»: «sentaos», «levantaos». STEP 7: the «tú» negative irregulars follow the «yo» present: «no digas», «no hagas», «no vayas», «no pongas», «no salgas», «no seas», «no tengas», «no vengas». STEP 8: in the negative, pronouns go before the verb, as separate words: «no me llames», «no te levantes», «no lo hagas». In the affirmative, they go after and attach: «llámame», «levántate», «hazlo».
em português, o imperativo negativo usa: English pronoun position never flips between affirmative and negative — "call me" and "don't call me" both keep the pronoun as its own word right after the verb. Spanish's switch — attached after the verb in the affirmative («llámame»), a separate word before the verb in the negative («no me llames») — is a genuinely new rule to track, on top of the subjunctive switch itself.

PASSO 1: instruções passo a passo (recei: STEP 1: step-by-step instructions (recipes, manuals) use the «tú» or «usted» imperative, in short sentences: «Corta las patatas», «Fríe el huevo». STEP 2: asking for something: the imperative with «por favor» is correct, but a question is often preferred to sound friendlier: «¿Puedes cerrar la puerta?» instead of «Cierra la puerta». STEP 3: inviting: the imperative is warm here, not a command: «Pasa», «Siéntate», «Come un poco más». STEP 4: words to get someone's attention in formal settings: «oiga» (excuse me, with «usted»), «perdone» or «disculpe» (sorry/excuse me), and «mire» (look). STEP 5: on signs and notices, the infinitive is used instead of the imperative: «Empujar», «Tirar», «No fumar», «Cerrar la puerta» — a genuinely different habit from English, which puts signs in the imperative too ("Push," "Pull," "No smoking") but Spanish prefers the plain infinitive form. STEP 6: watch two confusing look-alikes: «ve» is the imperative of «ir» («Ve a casa») and also of «ver» («Ve esta película»); context sorts it out. And «sal» is the imperative of «salir» («Sal ahora») and also means table salt. STEP 7: in Spain, «coge» (from coger) means "grab/catch," but in parts of Latin America the verb has a vulgar sense; to be safe everywhere, use «toma» or «agarra» instead. And remember that «pegar» in Spanish means to hit or to glue — never "to grab" or "to catch," even though it might look like it should. STEP 8: with «ustedes», the imperative works for any group: «Pasen, por favor.» In Spain, among friends, it's «Pasad».
em português, o imperativo é muito parec: English also uses the imperative on signs ("Push," "No smoking"), so that habit transfers fine — Spanish's preference for the bare infinitive instead («Empujar», «No fumar») is the one adjustment to make. The real trap is «pegar», which looks close enough to "peg" or could be mistaken for "to grab" — it actually means to hit or to glue. To say "grab it," reach for «toma» or «agarra» instead.

Para fazer uma tortilla de batatas para: To make a potato tortilla for four people, you need potatoes, eggs, oil, and salt. First peel the potatoes and cut them into small pieces. Put oil in a pan and fry the potatoes on low heat. Meanwhile, beat six eggs in a large bowl with a little salt. When the potatoes are soft, take them out of the oil and mix them with the eggs. Wait five minutes. Then put the mixture back in the pan and wait a bit. When it's golden on one side, flip it using a plate. Don't be afraid: with practice, it'll turn out well. When it's ready, serve it hot or cold.
